identification.summary: Storm-2077 is Microsoft's name for a China-based threat actor that Microsoft assesses has been active since at least January 2024 [S1]. Microsoft states Storm-2077 overlaps with activity other vendors track as TAG-100 [S1]. Recorded Future's Insikt Group first reported TAG-100 in July 2024, then re-designated it RedNovember in September 2025 and noted the overlap with Microsoft's Storm-2077 [S2][S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: active since at least January 2024 [S1]. Recorded Future: report on TAG-100 published July 2024; RedNovember activity window June 2024 to July 2025 [S2][S6].
identification.notes: Aliases: TAG-100 (Recorded Future, July 2024) and RedNovember (Recorded Future, September 2025) [S2][S6]. The overlap between Microsoft and Recorded Future clusters is stated as an overlap, not an identity, by Microsoft [S1]. Microsoft says Storm-2077 also shared some victimology and techniques with other actors it was already tracking, without naming them [S1].

attribution.sponsor: Microsoft assesses Storm-2077 is a China state threat actor [S1]. Recorded Future assesses RedNovember (formerly TAG-100) as highly likely Chinese state-sponsored, per coverage of its report [S6][S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft uses the wording 'assesses' for China state actor status and 'likely' for the intelligence-collection objective [S1]. In July 2024 Recorded Future could not attribute TAG-100 to a specific country but said the victim profile aligned with historical Chinese state-sponsored targeting [S2][S3]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft cites its own telemetry and analysis of activity affecting a handful of customers [S1]. Recorded Future cites victimology consistent with Chinese state-sponsored groups, later upgraded after further review [S2][S6].

objectives: Microsoft assesses Storm-2077 likely operates with the objective of intelligence collection [S1]. Email theft is a stated focus, since mailboxes can be analyzed later without immediate loss of access [S1].

sectors: Semiconductor supply chain and high-technology manufacturing
regions: Global, including at least ten countries in TAG-100 reporting [S2][S3]
Asia-Pacific intergovernmental organizations; Southeast Asia trade-focused body [S2][S6]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says Storm-2077 initially hit US government agencies and NGOs, then broadened to the defense industrial base, aviation, telecommunications, and financial and legal services, describing targeting as 'all sectors appear to be on the table' [S1]. Recorded Future's TAG-100 report listed two Asia-Pacific intergovernmental organization secretariats, diplomatic entities, ministries of foreign affairs, trade associations, and semiconductor supply-chain, non-profit and religious organizations [S2][S3]. The Record also reported religious organizations in the US and Taiwan and a political party supporting an investigation into the Chinese government [S4]. RedNovember coverage reports at least two US defense contractors and a European engine manufacturer [S6].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft describes credential-phishing for initial access, in some cases likely exploitation of edge-facing devices, reuse of valid credentials, and use of stolen credentials to reach legitimate cloud applications including eDiscovery applications to exfiltrate email; after gaining administrative access the actor created its own application with mail-read rights [S1]. Microsoft's page names no malware or CVEs [S1]. Recorded Future reports exploitation of internet-facing products including Citrix NetScaler, F5 BIG-IP, Zimbra, Microsoft Exchange, SonicWall, Cisco ASA, Palo Alto GlobalProtect and Fortinet FortiGate, with reconnaissance and attempted exploitation of dozens of US organizations after a proof-of-concept for CVE-2024-3400 was released [S2][S3]. Post-access tooling is open source: Pantegana and SparkRAT in TAG-100 reporting, and Pantegana, Cobalt Strike and SparkRAT in RedNovember reporting [S2][S3][S6][S7]. Later reporting adds Ivanti Connect Secure, Sophos and Outlook Web Access as targeted access points [S6]. Recorded Future argues open-source tooling complicates attribution and lets state actors outsource to proxy groups or contractors [S2][S3].

Reconnaissance and exploitation attempts against dozens of US organizations followed the CVE-2024-3400 proof-of-concept release [S2][S3][S4].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft describes Storm-2077 phishing, eDiscovery cloud-app credential abuse, and creation of a mail-read application for email exfiltration, and notes TAG-100 overlap [S1].

campaigns.summary: Insikt Group assesses the cluster as highly likely Chinese state-sponsored and reports broadened targeting of US defense contractors, aerospace, semiconductors and government networks through firewalls, VPNs and OWA, with an analysis cut-off of 25 July 2025 [S5][S6][S7].

diamond.adversary: China-based state threat actor per Microsoft; highly likely Chinese state-sponsored per Recorded Future [S1][S6]. Operator identities, organization and tasking authority are not public in the sources gathered.
diamond.capability: Credential phishing, edge-device exploitation, cloud application abuse for mail access, and open-source implants (Pantegana, SparkRAT, Cobalt Strike) [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Recorded Future reporting describes C2 for open-source tooling; specific IPs, domains and hosting details were not obtainable from the sources opened here [S2].
diamond.victim: Government, NGO, defense industrial base, aviation, telecommunications, finance, legal, semiconductor and intergovernmental organizations [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection for a PRC state objective as assessed by Microsoft; victim set includes entities tied to Asia-Pacific diplomacy and Taiwan-related religious groups [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing VPN, firewall and mail gateways; cloud email and eDiscovery applications; weak control of application registrations with mail-read permissions [S1][S2][S6].

gaps: Recorded Future's RedNovember report (PDF) and original TAG-100 report could not be opened directly; details come from search excerpts and secondary coverage (The Hacker News, The Record, The Register) [S2][S5][S6][S7].
WebFetch failed for recordedfuture.com, thehackernews.com and theregister.com (host not resolved), so those pages were not read in full.
Microsoft's page names no tools, CVEs, indicators or victims for Storm-2077; the overlap with TAG-100/RedNovember is stated by Microsoft as an overlap only [S1].

Microsoft does not name the other actors whose victimology and techniques Storm-2077 overlapped; one secondary summary claims overlap with Silk Typhoon (HAFNIUM) but this was not verified in a primary source.
A CyCraft report on RedNovember expansion (mentioning a LESLIELOADER loader) appeared in search but could not be searched or opened; its claims are unverified.
Infrastructure indicators, exact CVE list exploited, and the full victim count are not verified here.
No government attribution or sanctions/indictments were found; sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA, contractor) is unknown.
Activity after the 25 July 2025 report cut-off is not covered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing VPNs, firewalls and mail gateways, and cloud email tenants including eDiscovery applications [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 2: The actor has expanded from US government and NGOs to the defense industrial base, aviation and semiconductors, so DoD contractors are within the target set [S1][S6]. STEP 3: The observed template is edge-device exploitation or credential phishing, then open-source implants (Pantegana, SparkRAT, Cobalt Strike) or cloud-app abuse, then mailbox collection [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued intelligence collection against DIB, aerospace and allied government email. MDCOA is rapid exploitation of a newly disclosed edge-device vulnerability across DoD-adjacent organizations soon after proof-of-concept release, as seen with CVE-2024-3400 [S2][S3]. Candidate indicators: new application registrations with mail-read permissions, unusual eDiscovery application sign-ins, Pantegana or SparkRAT artifacts on hosts behind edge devices, and exploitation attempts against VPN and firewall appliances [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track edge-device advisories and cloud tenant audit logs for application consent and mail-read grants, since these are the observed collection mechanisms [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: cloud tenant and perimeter device hardening and hunt actions fall to the system owner; coordinate approvals before remediation on contractor systems. (3) Mission assurance: email holds credentials, financial and intellectual-property data, so assess exposure of mission planning traffic to mailbox compromise [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DIB partners and DC3, and note that vendor names differ (Storm-2077, RedNovember, TAG-100) so reporting should be deconflicted [S1][S6].

provenance.importedSummary: TAG-100 is a cyber-espionage APT that targets government and private sector organizations globally, exploiting vulnerabilities in internet-facing devices such as Citrix NetScaler and F5 BIG-IP for initial access. The group employs open-source tools like Pantegana and SparkRAT for persistence and post-exploitation activities, including credential theft and email data exfiltration. TAG-100 has compromised entities in at least ten countries, including two Asia-Pacific intergovernmental organizations, and focuses on sectors like education, finance, and local government. Their operations highlight the challenges of attribution due to the use of off-the-shelf tools and techniques that overlap with other state-sponsored groups.
